source.title: NeurFlow: Interpreting Neural Networks through Neuron Groups and Functional Interactions
source.authors: T. M. Cao; Nhat Hoang; Hieu H. Pham; Phi Le Nguyen; My T. Thai

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether circuits built from a model's own neurons have functional fidelity, using neuron masking and retention on CNNs rather than the attribution-graph and reconstruction-error method in V5.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses polysemantic neurons and proposes neuron-group circuits, but reports no measurements of Qwen3 neuron poles, language-model explanation accuracy, Inception cat-and-car examples, or automated explanation scores. The fidelity results below bear on the broader neuron-circuit sufficiency question in V5, but do not measure attribution-graph reconstruction error.
record.test_reason: The study builds circuits from neurons of small ImageNet CNNs (ResNet50, GoogLeNet) and reports how well its own core-neuron selection performs. Masking or retaining NeurFlow's selected neurons is compared with random neurons, which measures method performance. It does not test V5's subject: attribution graphs over a large model's own neurons, compared against a trained replacement model and its reconstruction error. It assumes rather than measures neuron polysemanticity, so it bears on no version's numbers. The record's T2 'tests V5' reading is too generous.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors present NeurFlow as an automated framework that finds core concept neurons, groups them, and quantifies group interactions with fidelity in CNNs. They motivate groups as the unit because single neurons are polysemantic. They note limits: a CNN focus and top-k activation concepts.
record.recipe_differences: The study constructs CNN circuits from core concept neurons, groups them by visual concepts, and evaluates fidelity through masking and retention. It does not use the attribution-graph method or report reconstruction error.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports a trade-off with tau: smaller tau can make retained-model performance more unstable. It also studies single-layer versus multi-layer settings. For the added-neuron experiment, the reported exception is GoogLeNet layer 5b.

fits_no_version.finding: In ResNet50 and GoogLeNet, masking NeurFlow-selected core neurons (tau 4–16) drops accuracy far more than masking random neurons. Retaining only them preserves accuracy much better. Adding 50% more neurons barely helps, except +25% at GoogLeNet 5b.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small ImageNet CNNs, a sparse set of neurons chosen by integrated-gradient attribution forms a circuit that largely preserves classification behaviour without a replacement model.

record.problems: The evaluation is on ResNet50 and GoogLeNet vision models, not language models. The fidelity evidence is based on accuracy changes under masking or retention, not reconstruction error; many plotted comparisons have no numerical values in the text. The paper notes a trade-off with tau and focuses on CNNs and top-k activation concepts.
record.rows_left_out: No additional V5-relevant results were omitted. Other reported experiments, including core-neuron optimality, attribution-score correlations, method comparisons, and image-debugging examples, do not directly measure whether the circuit explains model behavior without a replacement model.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit shares; no language models studied.
Shares across language-model families and scales.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons. The paper assumes CNN neurons are polysemantic (citing Olah/Cammarata) without testing pose or recursive generalization.
No interpretable-neuron shares across tools or architectures.
Attribution graphs over a large model's own neurons, compared with replacement models and their reconstruction error.
Whether top-k activating-example explanations predict firing elsewhere. Top-k concepts are acknowledged only as a limitation.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V5 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are dropped. The rows are the study's own method against a random baseline, in small vision CNNs rather than a large model. No replacement-model or reconstruction-error comparison is made. The paper's stance (neurons polysemantic, use groups) leans against the essay's framing but provides no measurement of polysemantic share. The text says 'retraining' for random neurons, apparently a typo for retaining.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B audit shares and tested explanations on held-out activations.
Language-model neuron-pole shares across model families, architectures, and scales.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization.
Interpretable-neuron shares across tools or architectures, the proposed causes of messy late-layer neurons, and the InceptionV1-sized estimates.
The study uses CNN neuron-group circuits rather than attribution graphs, and does not report reconstruction error or test a large language model.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict firing on separate examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Mask core concept neurons and compare model accuracy with masking equal numbers of random neurons.
rows.value: Masking core concept neurons consistently caused a more pronounced performance decline than masking random neurons.
rows.locator: Section 4, Fidelity of core concept neurons; Figure 5
rows.note: The paper describes results across the tested tau and layer settings; Figure 5 presents separate plotted results, but the text does not give their numerical values.
rows.check: Compares the study's own core-neuron selection with random neurons in a CNN, which is method performance. No large model, attribution graph or replacement-model comparison. Values exist only in Figure 5.

rows.subject: GoogLeNet
rows.operation_detail: Mask core concept neurons and compare model accuracy with masking equal numbers of random neurons.
rows.value: Masking core concept neurons consistently caused a more pronounced performance decline than masking random neurons; at layer 5a, accuracy fell to nearly 0.
rows.locator: Section 4, Fidelity of core concept neurons; Figure 5
rows.note: The paper describes results across the tested tau and layer settings; Figure 5 presents separate plotted results, but the text does not give their numerical values.
rows.check: Same as R1 (GoogLeNet). The layer-5a near-zero accuracy is a textual description of a plot.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Retain only core concept neurons and compare accuracy with retaining equal numbers of random neurons.
rows.baseline: Retaining equal numbers of random neurons
rows.value: Retaining only core concept neurons preserved model performance substantially better than retaining random neurons.
rows.locator: Section 4, Fidelity of core concept neurons; Figure 5
rows.note: Figure 5 shows separate plotted results; the paper's text gives the qualitative comparison rather than numerical values.
rows.check: Retention fidelity of the study's own selected neurons versus random; method performance in a CNN, not V5's setting. Text says smaller tau gives unstable retention.

rows.subject: GoogLeNet
rows.operation_detail: Retain only core concept neurons and compare accuracy with retaining equal numbers of random neurons.
rows.baseline: Retaining equal numbers of random neurons
rows.value: Retaining only core concept neurons preserved model performance substantially better than retaining random neurons.
rows.locator: Section 4, Fidelity of core concept neurons; Figure 5
rows.note: Figure 5 shows separate plotted results; the paper's text gives the qualitative comparison rather than numerical values.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Add 50% more non-core neurons, selected by NeuronMCT scores, to the core concept neuron set.
rows.baseline: Core concept neurons without the added non-core neurons
rows.value: Adding non-core neurons had little to no effect on improving model performance.
rows.locator: Section 4, Fidelity of core concept neurons; Appendix D.6; Figure 17
rows.note: The reported comparison concerns adding neurons to the proposed set; it is not a direct reconstruction-error measurement.
rows.check: A completeness check of the study's own selection (adding NeuronMCT-ranked neurons). It is not a reconstruction-error measure. Appendix D.6 applies it to both retaining and masking.

rows.subject: GoogLeNet
rows.operation_detail: Add 50% more non-core neurons, selected by NeuronMCT scores, to the core concept neuron set.
rows.baseline: Core concept neurons without the added non-core neurons
rows.value: Adding 50% more non-core neurons improved model performance by 25% at layer 5b in the retaining setup.
rows.note: The paper describes this as the exception among the tested extension settings.
rows.check: The exception to the completeness check: +25% accuracy at GoogLeNet layer 5b, retaining. It is method performance, not V5.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ResNet50 and GoogLeNet core-neuron fidelity experiments
reader_labels.reason: Core-neuron masking affected accuracy more than random-neuron masking, and retaining core neurons preserved performance better than retaining random neurons (R1–R4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Adding non-core neurons to the core set
reader_labels.reason: The reported effects were generally small for ResNet50, but adding neurons improved GoogLeNet retaining performance by 25% at layer 5b (R5–R6).
